prerequisites: Familiarity with elementary concepts from strength of materials, particularly stresses, strains, and Hooke's law.
Familiarity with elementary concepts related to mass transport, particularly conservation laws of mass and momentum, advective and diffusive transport.
Familiarity with the meaning of ordinary and partial differential equations and their solution in the case of linear first-order equations.
Ability to perform stability analysis of a system of linear first-order ordinary differential equations.
Basic knowledge in physiology and cell biology.

learning_outcomes.text: The student can construct a mathematical model of physiological systems and processes. From a qualitative description of the various biological components and their interactions, they are able to set up a system of mathematical equations. Depending on the nature of the system or process, as well as the objectives of the model, this may involve a system of algebraic, ordinary, or partial differential equations. Crucial here is the translation and application of generic basic knowledge (mechanics, strength of materials, mass transport, chemical reactions, etc.) to concrete and usable models to quantitatively describe a physiological system or process.

In the case of simple algebraic and ordinary differential equations, the student can solve the models and perform a stability analysis. The student can critically interpret the results in the context of the physiological system or process.

syllabus_topics: Construction, solution, and analysis of compartment models of physiological systems and processes, relevant for a quantitative study of, for example, digestion, respiration, kidneys, liver, and endocrine system, as well as their use in pharmacy (pharmacokinetic models).

Construction, solution, and analysis of models of physicochemical phenomena in electrically excitable cells, including modeling the dynamics of ion channels and action potentials, relevant for a quantitative study of the nervous system.

Modeling of tissue dynamic processes using partial differential equations and agent-based models, relevant for the quantitative study of tissue and organ development (morphogenesis, embryonic development), growth and regeneration of tissues, as well as tumor growth.
Students learn to construct mathematical models of physiological systems and processes themselves, solve them, and perform stability analysis where possible.
